introduction: These readings set the Word of God against the limits of the human mind. However high thought may soar, it cannot reach the divine Essence, for the encompassed cannot comprehend what encompasses it; the Word is a cup whose wine is hidden meaning; and its understanding depends on purity of heart, not learning, which can be 'the most grievous of all veils'. Bahá’u’lláh therefore reproaches the learned and the sects who heard the verses and turned away, answers objections to his writings, and says that on this Day sciences and books will not avail. Closing passages add that every human statement of the teachings is limited by the one who makes it. A hundred of the guide's hundred and eighty-eight quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Isaiah's 'my thoughts are not your thoughts', Job, Paul on the wisdom of the world and on knowing in part, Jesus thanking God for what is hidden from the wise, the Tao Te Ching, the Cloud of Unknowing, Pascal, the Qur'an's challenge to produce its like. Ten push back or add a side: Locke's 'reason must be our last judge', Kant's 'dare to know', Milton on opinion as knowledge in the making, Mill, Tennyson's honest doubt, Paine, Proverbs' 'get wisdom', Aristotle on the desire to know, Pascal's thinking reed, and Montaigne on interpreting interpretations.
questions: 'The all-encompassing must be greater than that which is encompassed.' What follows for any human account of God?
Why might knowledge be 'the most grievous of all veils'? Is it learning that veils, or something that tends to come with it? Compare Milton and Proverbs.
The readings say understanding the Word depends on purity of heart, not on learning. What part is left for study?
Locke and Kant make reason the judge. The readings place the Word beyond the intellect's reach. How do you decide what to believe about a claim like that?
Tennyson found more faith in honest doubt than in half the creeds. Do the readings leave room for it?
The last readings say every human statement of the teachings is limited. How should that affect the way believers speak, including in a study guide?

outside.why: Isaiah has God say: as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my thoughts than your thoughts.
A psalm says: the voice of the Lord is powerful; the voice of the Lord is full of majesty.
A psalm says: how sweet are thy words unto my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth.
The Dhammapada says that one word of sense, which quiets the hearer, is better than a thousand senseless words.
Paul would rather speak five words with his understanding than ten thousand in an unknown tongue.
Zophar asks Job: canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
Paul exclaims at the depth of the wisdom of God: how unsearchable are his judgments.
Pascal turned the figure round: by space the universe encompasses me, and by thought I comprehend it. Can the encompassed in any sense hold what encompasses it?
John's Gospel begins: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.
The Qur'an says that though the sea became ink for the words of the Lord, the sea would be exhausted first.
A psalmist says: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
God tells Moses: thou canst not see my face, for there shall no man see me, and live.
The Qur'an says: vision comprehendeth him not, but he comprehendeth all vision.
Xenophanes said that if oxen and horses could paint, they would paint the gods like oxen and horses.
Pascal wrote that if there is a God he is infinitely incomprehensible, having no affinity to us.
Paul says: now we see through a glass, darkly; now I know in part.
Job says: these are parts of his ways, but how little a portion is heard of him.
Hamlet tells his friend there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in his philosophy.
The Qur'an says: We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves.
Locke held that reason must be our last judge and guide in every thing. If the intellect errs, what judges the claim that something lies beyond it?
Paul gave the same warning in a line: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Paul asks where the wise and the scribe are, since the world by wisdom knew not God.
Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent, and revealing them unto babes.
Ecclesiastes says that of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
Paul says his preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit.
Paul warns: beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit.
The Tao Te Ching says that he who knows does not speak, and he who speaks does not know.
The Cloud of Unknowing says that of God himself can no man think, and chooses to love what cannot be thought.
Milton held that where there is much desire to learn there will be much arguing and many opinions, for opinion in good men is knowledge in the making. Is learning the veil, or only pride in it?
Proverbs says: wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom. How does that command stand beside 'the most grievous of all veils is the veil of knowledge'?
The Qur'an says people have broken their religion into sects, each group rejoicing in its tenets.
Jesus said: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.
John says he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
A psalm says: the Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him in truth.
Jesus called some teachers blind leaders of the blind, and said both shall fall into the ditch.
The Pharisees asked, as an argument: have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?
John's Gospel says: light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.
Jesus wept over a city that did not know the things which belong unto its peace.
Jeremiah says the people have forsaken the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns that hold no water.
Paul says that when the old scriptures are read, a vail remaineth upon the heart of some readers.
Isaiah is told of a people whose heart is fat, whose ears are heavy, and whose eyes are shut.
Jesus said: seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.
Amos cried woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria.
Jesus spoke of those who honour dead prophets and say they would never have opposed them.
Paul prays that the eyes of his readers' understanding may be enlightened.
The boy Samuel was taught to answer: speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth.
Two disciples said afterwards: did not our heart burn within us, while he opened to us the scriptures?
God asks Job: who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?
Mill wrote that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. What is lost if the learned lay down their pens?
Jeremiah says: thy words were found, and I did eat them; thy word was the joy and rejoicing of mine heart.
A psalm calls: O sing unto the Lord a new song; sing unto the Lord, all the earth.
John's Gospel speaks of the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
The Qur'an likens a goodly word to a goodly tree, its root set firm, its branches reaching into heaven.
A psalm says: the heavens declare the glory of God; night unto night sheweth knowledge.
The officers sent to seize Jesus returned saying: never man spake like this man.
The Qur'an makes the same challenge: though mankind and the jinn should assemble, they could not produce the like of it.
Paine held that what is revelation to the first person is hearsay to every other. Is the beauty or power of a text evidence of where it came from?
Jesus said the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and they that hear shall live.
Hebrews calls the word of God quick and powerful, sharper than any twoedged sword.
Israel's confession begins with a command to listen: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.
James says: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Jesus said: there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.
A psalmist says: thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
Isaiah calls: arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.
He that sat upon the throne in the Apocalypse says: behold, I make all things new.
Jesus said: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden.
A psalm says: this is the day which the Lord hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
A psalm says: thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
John's Gospel says that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
Hearers of Jesus asked how he knew letters, having never learned, and he answered: my doctrine is not mine.
Jesus said: think not that I am come to destroy the law or the prophets; I am come to fulfil.
Jesus said: neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet.
Jesus lamented over a city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to her.
Jesus compared the one who hears and does to a house on rock, which fell not when the floods came.
James says that he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea, driven with the wind and tossed.
Tennyson wrote of a friend: there lives more faith in honest doubt, believe me, than in half the creeds. Are doubts always something to beware of?
In the parable some seed is choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life.
Paul wrote that now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
Isaiah says to the God of Israel: verily thou art a God that hidest thyself.
Exodus tells how the people, while Moses was on the mountain, made a molten calf and worshipped it.
Jesus said: no man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.
Mark says that when they were alone, Jesus expounded all things to his disciples.
The Qur'an says its verses are of two kinds, the clear, which are the substance of the Book, and the allegorical.
Jeremiah says: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his riches.
Aristotle said that all men by nature desire to know. Is that desire one of the things that 'shall not profit you in this day', or a gift to be used?
Paul counted all he had learned and been as loss beside the knowledge of Christ.
Jesus charged the teachers with holding the tradition of men and laying aside the commandment of God.
Kant's motto was: have courage to use your own reason. How does 'cast away what ye possess' differ from asking people to stop thinking?
Paul says that faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Paul calls his troubles a light affliction, which is but for a moment.
Jesus said: enter ye in at the strait gate, for narrow is the way which leadeth unto life.
James says that every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.
The merchant in the parable found one pearl of great price, and sold all that he had.
Augustine calls God most hidden and most near, and cannot finish the list.
Acts praises the Bereans, who received the word with readiness of mind and searched the scriptures daily.
Peter writes that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
Montaigne observed that there is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things. Where does interpretation stop?
Paul says: we know in part, and we prophesy in part; what is in part shall be done away.
Tennyson wrote that our little systems have their day and cease to be: they are but broken lights.
